title: sir, you are being hunted
text: “It's a great game that will take up an afternoon, but for 20 bucks? At its current state, which it will most likely have forever, it is worth 5 dollars, there is just not enough content to justify such a price.” I liked this game a lot, It took me just less than 4 hours beat, and I enjoyed every minute. I do think it is telling that nobody who reviewed this game seems to have more than 20 hours. Overall the game reminded me of the excellent game “Undying” The Story There is not much to the story but it is there. It starts you off with a storyboard, which makes little sense. You can find books, letters and plaques, with a few hints to the story. Nothing is really clear, other than that the stonehenge can weaken the barriers to other worlds -don’t say it's magic-. I don't think it is very fitting, however. The Graphics People complain about the graphics in this, and they are not very realistic. I think they are nice and stylised and reminded me much of “undying”. There is fog, and it’s all not very colourful, but I think the graphics well suit the game. There was graphical errors, but these had little effect and I think it is because it is randomly generated. the robots and houses and such look appealing, the ground and the rocks could use some work. There is fog, and I can see some people being bothered by that, however you can still make out things in the distance clearly. The Gameplay There are a few weapons(pistol, shotgun, rifle, blunderbuss, axe) which is a good thing, as inventory management is a big thing, and there is little space for many weapons and an effective load of ammo. Each has a defined purpose, and there is nothing else fitting that could be added and not feel unnecessary. It took me awhile to get used to combat, as the sensitivity was strange at all levels. New items don’t spawn in, which mean you can’t play around in one place too long. Some enemies are unkillable, and over all it feels like you are meant to avoid all enemies. Despite being open world and randomly generated, it has low replayability. I blame this on the fact it has only one mode, a scavenger hunt . The game starts you off the center island, with an equal in size island to the north, east, south and west of you which you can go to at anytime by finding a dock in the direction of the island you want to go to. The goal is to find 20 or something gems, which you need to put into the stonehenge to win. These gems are scattered around the islands. There are number of enemy types that randomly patrol the islands, the more gems you return, the more enemies will spawn. There are towns and other building with loot scattered around the islands. Depending on the class you can start with almost nothing, but with luck you can have a ton of good loot fast. You can store found loot in the buildings without fear of them despawning. It took me only a hour or so to realise you can also stash gems in buildings, so the game does not spawn in more enemies. You can find maps, which you can use to mark 3 spots. 3 spots is more than enough, as it allows you to mark 2 towns where you stashed goodies and a final one for the dock. Your position appears on the map, so navigation with one is real easy. The gems produce smoke which can be seen from far away, but even then there was some frustrating times where I could not find the final gem on an island. Once a robot patrol finds a gem, 2 of them, and a robot dog guard it. Only the first and most basic robot hunters guard gems, and so it is not hard to just shoot them and take the gem. Gems are normally far off the beaten path, so robot patrols will to too long to arrive if you move fast. Alternatively you can throw a clock or bottle as a distraction, but this is far harder to pull off and more risky in my mind than violence. The fact only basic robots guard means you only have to encounter these basic robots, as you can just hide from the other, perhaps cooler types. It was easy for me in the final hours of this game, to make a safe point and stash near the dock of an island, and then find and retrieve the gems with ammo to spare. Mechanics -Stealth Not like most games, there is no sneaking up behind people and stabbing them in the neck or what not (there is no one hit melee). Rather you are more like a powerless convict running from police. Areas are randomly patrolled, and there are a few options of distracting enemies. This is hard to do, and sometimes it feels just easier to kill them. The game does not pause when you loot, so distractions are even worse. There is bunch of guarded items you need to collect, I think only 2 of which I used a distraction. Some other reviewer said this game was more like guerrilla warfare, you hide, shoot a few shots, pick something up then run away. -Combat Once you get used to it, it feels good. The health system is very forgiving, but once you run out of rags(which do not respawn) to bandage, you are dead. Eating food frequently will allow to regain health. The guns are powerful, but lack range, even for the sniper. Ammo and guns are rare, yet almost necessary. There is an ADS function that greatly improves damage and accuracy. Going in guns blazing never really works even on small groups later in the game, and if you chose a real class, you will only have a gun by then. If there is something you really want, you can try to sneak up to it, distract the guards or pick one off, hide, pick another one off, hide…. It is repetitive, but also fun. -Inventory You can keep thing in homes without them despawning, so you are encouraged to keep caches of food and ammo in easy to reach spots. Nothing knew spawns in, yet you can discard things, so watch out. There are 3 types of loot: junk, dubious and useable. Junk does nothing, dubious hurts your hunger when used, and useable is what you want. I at first wondered why there was useless items, but I figure it is to keep you looting and exposed longer. People complain about not being able to go in homes, yet being able to enter them would ruin the game. It is never worth it to kill every one guarding lootables, so you need to sneak up on them, and loot what you can quickly before you are seen, to be able to enter the homes would break this. Judging whether it is worth the risk is one of the biggest aspects about this game. Horror The game was unconventionally scary just like its stealth. It is “you hide behind a stone wall as a clunky robot flies past, wondering to yourself if it will see you” kind of scary, no jump scares or anything. The point of the game is to avoid enemies, you never really encounter these scary enemies up close, limiting the thrill of the game. I think more horror would have improved this game. Other Notes Over all it is a beautiful game, I just love to see a line of hunters march in a line through the long grass. However it is kind of niche, and the novelty of it wears off once you finish your first play thru. There is just not enough game for it to be worth 20$. I encountered no bugs, and it felt finished.  It took me 4 hours to beat it, and I was not rushing. The Devs claim the game has replayability do to its randomness, however when the game is so straightforward do to its one goal and limited supplies, that replayability is questionable. The is no other modes. There is starting classes, and that's all to make each game different, other than the map not being the same. This game is dying for more modes. It's a great game that will take up an afternoon, but for 20 bucks? At its current state, which it will most likely have forever, it is worth 5 dollars, there is just not enough content to justify such a price.

text: I give this game thumbs up because I appreciate the idea of it, and want to support developers trying to do something different. Yet, it was a mixed experience overall. My biggest issues were; 1)The trailer is quite misleading. The game has pretty gloomy and dark atmosphere, not comical as the trailer was. So my initial feeling was disappointment, because game was nothing that the trailer made it look to be. But eventually, the atmosphere of the game stands on its own. Just be prepared that the game is not as funny as the trailer. 2)I didnt feel that the procedural system adds anything to the game. The environments are made randomly for each playthrough, but there is not enough variery in the landscape patterns to make any worthwhile differences via procedural system. Its the same barren lands, and having the same trees in little different places doesnt really enchant the gameplay. The game is not a roguelike either. When you die (and you die very easily), you dont start the game from a 0, but just load a checkpoint. This imho kills the point of randomly generated world, since you dont need to really adapt into new world every time you play it, like you would do in Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy, Spelunky, etc. In this game, I kept thinking that it would be much better, if the open world was well planned solid world full of unique situations, instead of a procedural world. 3)Sneaking is too hard, and too punishing. The distances in the game are very very long, and most of the gametime you will be running from point A to B, without really sneaking. But when you reach a point where you "must" sneak, often its better just to shoot the enemy who is in your way, and run away as fast as you can. Doing proper sneaking can take a lot, lot of time, and getting spotted by enemy when too near to them is almost 100% death to you, which will mean a lot and lot of time wasted due to rare checkpoints. If you run and gun instead, you will lose only a 1-2 minutes of your time (most spent on running), instead of 10-20 minutes you would spend trying to sneak properly. Overall I was somewhat disappointed with the game, but liked the idea and style of it enough, that I wish the developers move into a new interesting and unique projects soon. Apparently this game is getting a multiplayer someday, but IMHO its waste of time of the devs, and they should just make a new game instead. For time being, I can still recommend this game to the people who are fascinated by the idea, even though it has its share of problems.

text: Contrary to popular belief, and unlike the title suggests, no, you are not being hunted. Instead its a treasure hunt as you sift through un-enterable buildings, collecting 7/10 useless things, and 3/10 that might actually be of use. Bots, while their dialogue amused me, and their aggression towards you is something to consider, aren't as amazing as the blurb suggests either. I scrapped one with an axe and it bunny-hopped backwards away from me, continuously, until I finally managed to end him with another swing. I don't get why they try to escape you like that when they could very easily put you down. The terrain is vast and mostly uninteresting. At one point I roamed so much of an island undisturbed I actually thought a glitch had ejected all bots from the map. This game would be cool if you were actually being constantly hounded by hunting parties that are out looking for you, so the stakes would be that much higher. But instead it's just a matter of working through (or around) the various patrols to get at the supposed plot devices while fending off periodic starvation. I find that the game description is... slightly misleading.

title: slender: the arrival
text: After playing the Eight Pages, I was unbelievably stoked for this game, expecting dynamic gameplay through twists and turns of psychological horror and atmosphere. And to be honest, the game didn't FAIL, but it's not worth $10. First off, the game is disappointingly short, with a total of 5 levels with actual interactive content, if that. Even though the first "level" does a good job of introducing the uncertain atmosphere of what you're entering into, it's still just a prologue. The second level is the age-old Eight Pages level that's been improved on. I can honestly say that they did an excellent job of making you feel completely lost and helpless in the woods even more so than the freeware version did, so props to the developers on that level. The third level is basically a more aggravating variation of the second, and the fourth level is essentially you walking down a linear path set by the game. The fifth level is pretty fun, too, but I won't spoil what happens it that one. The second thing I disliked about this game is the ungodly difficulty. I enjoyed the atmosphere of the second level, but it was still balls-hard for me to complete. I felt like I had to get lucky enough to a.) actually find the page in the place I was looking and b.) not turn around to see Slender Man standing right next to me. I heard somewhere that the Eight Pages level in The Arrival was supposed to be easier than the freeware version, but I found it just as hard. The third level is where is gets unbearable. You're trapped in an underground site of sorts with an unknown creature chasing you around, and you have to activate 6 power modules (or something like that) to get the elevator working and escape. Consider this an more frustrating version of the Eight Pages; by this time, the atmosphere is replaced by unbridled rage as you have to cross your fingers and hope that this time, when you roll the dice, you'll HAPPEN to find the generator and have enough time to make it back before the Chaser pops out from around the corner and beats the tar outta you. Practice did jack-squat for me; one run I'll get 5 activated, the next run I'll get one activated. And it's not like I died prematurely either; I'll be running around for half an hour unable to get more than 3 generators before the Chaser finally finishes me off. In fact, I'm pretty sure the run where I won was one of my shortest runs. Words cannot express my emotion when I beat that level. The fifth level wasn't as much as tough as just completely confusing as what you were supposed to do to survive. That level was fun once I got the hang of it, but before then I was basically flailing angrily. Bottom line: The Arrival is a small, one-and-done game. The experience is very real, but it's also very short-lived and can quickly be replaced by frustration (which really isn't the point of a horror game). If this was $5 or less, I would say it be worth a shot if you had the money to throw around. For $10, however, you're definitely better off getting something better like Amnesia.

text: Slender the Arrival does it's best to give you a creepy experience but it just keeps falling flat. It is a very nonintuitive game. It's standard first person shooter controls (without the shooter) and places you in the creepy woods of a park. One of its main shortcomings is that it lacks the ability to deliver the story properly. We are supposed to make assumptions about everything. Assumptions that are probably wrong. I kept finding clues about a person and assumed that person might be me. Then it took reading some backstory in a walkthru to discover that I was a completely different person baguely mentioned in one of the notes. The first few times I played it I was throughly creeped out and some of the presentation helped with that. It uses a method of "steady-cam" view that looks like you are filming this which can also be viewed that you are someone else watching this person's footage (a la Blair Witch Project, CLoverfield, or Paranormal Activity). What you find does heighten the tension and when odd things are seen it really creeps you out. But then it feels like a grind. Where am I supposed to go next you ask. Oh over there. Wait I think I've found everything. Do I go back? Where to next? There is a decisivve lack of direction and instruction. It gave me a goal but the goal was so vague that I didn't know whether I was finished nor did I know if I was finding the right things. I wandered around doing nothing SLOWLY for a half hour and then quit the game. Why? HEre is the biggeswt problem. There is no save feature. It saves once you finish "THE CHAPTER". I was stuck in the "prologue" for days. Every time I tried it I had to start from the beginning. So by the 15th time I tried finding all the clues or whatever I was not afraid of the woods nor the creepy things. So far all I've seen are creepy things but none of them are harmful things. Don't get me wrong. This game has figured out that in horror you can't just in-your-face all the horror like Dead Space or Doom 3 etc. But it has to be subtle. But it hasn't fuguyred out pacing, story, furthering the adventure. It also relies a lot on camera glitches and sound effects and music. THose things are very important in horror. But in this case I am never sure if these elements actually appear in the game world or just in the game "providing atmosphere" like I'm being followed around by a 40s radio SFX guy banging pots together and breathing heavily. It reminds me of the scares in the movie The Ring where Ehren Krueger hit us over the head with loud noises and in your face weird cut in pictures to scare us and when you got to the end all you could say was "Huh?" I would be interested if this studio tried it again with horror as this was an improvement over its predecessor but it still isn't there. The controls and gameplay are still lacking. Your RUNNING mode isn't much faster than your WALKING mode. You can neither jump nor go in water so you feel like a child in one of those wheelie guides. The story needs a bit of polish. There needs to be a definite indication who I am and what I'm doing and how far I've gotten with it. Because leaving it up to my imagination is unacceptable in a game. How am _I_ supposed to know when I am done with a chapter if I don't know what I'm supposed to be looking for, etc. This will keep you entertained for a couple playthroughs until you give up and look through the readthroughs. (which don't really help as the items keep moving around) You want to get really scared, go for Five Nights at Freddy's.
